title: Sell Mineral Rights in Pleasant Valley, WV

metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Pleasant Valley, WV
metaDescription: Pleasant Valley, Marion County mineral owners: Fairmont-adjacent legacy wells, residential-lot severances, and courthouse heirship checks.
heroLead: Pleasant Valley sits just outside Fairmont in Marion County, where growing residential development sits over mineral estates severed well before the current houses went up.
intro: As Fairmont's suburban footprint has grown, Pleasant Valley has filled in with residential and commercial development, while the underlying mineral acreage — much of it severed generations ago — continues to be tracked separately at the Marion County Courthouse.

sections.heading: Residential growth over severed minerals
paragraphs: Owning a house or commercial lot in Pleasant Valley doesn't necessarily mean owning the minerals beneath it; many of these estates were split apart decades before the current surface development existed, and the mineral owner today is frequently an unrelated party or a family that moved away long ago.

sections.heading: Legacy wells near the Route 250 corridor
paragraphs: Pleasant Valley's proximity to Fairmont and the Route 250 development corridor means some tracts here carry both older Big Injun-era wellbores and interest from newer Marcellus leasing rounds. Confirming which applies to your specific parcel takes a title check rather than an assumption based on the neighborhood.

sections.heading: Reconciling a subdivision plat with an older mineral severance
paragraphs: Pleasant Valley's newer subdivisions were platted using modern surveying conventions that don't always align cleanly with the metes-and-bounds descriptions used in older mineral severance deeds. A parcel that looks like a single lot on a current plat map might correspond to only part of a larger historical mineral tract, or vice versa.
Sorting this out is a title task, and it's worth doing before assuming your current property lines match whatever mineral interest, if any, was reserved when the land was originally severed.

faqs.question: Do I own the minerals under my Pleasant Valley property?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily — check whether your deed includes a mineral reservation or whether the minerals were severed by a previous owner before your purchase.

faqs.question: How do I find out if my family holds a severed interest near Pleasant Valley?
faqs.answer: A Marion County Courthouse records search under your family name will confirm whether an interest exists separate from the current surface ownership.

faqs.question: Is Pleasant Valley near active drilling?
faqs.answer: It's close to Fairmont's Route 250 corridor, where both legacy and newer Marcellus leasing activity have occurred on surrounding tracts.

faqs.question: Does my subdivision lot match the original mineral severance boundaries?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily — modern plats and older severance deeds use different survey conventions, so this needs to be confirmed by a title review rather than assumed.

faqs.question: What if my Pleasant Valley property deed makes no mention of minerals at all?
faqs.answer: Silence in a deed doesn't necessarily mean no mineral rights exist or were reserved; a full title search tracing back through prior conveyances is the only way to confirm the actual status.
